doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Classical bass study with Roberts, Proto and O'Brien
summary: He took up the bow after his father's example and studied with Harold Roberts, Frank Proto and Orin O'Brien; Gene Bertoncini pushed him to play bow in public.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You must have got significant classical training in the conservatory?

I did. I didn’t stay in the conservatory that long, but when I first started playing the bass I was thumping around on it, and thinking I was getting pretty good. My father brought home a bow, and he said, “Here, try it with this.” And it was so depressing when he did it. I didn’t touch the bass for about two weeks, and I really thought, do I really want to do this? And he said, “Well if you’re going to play the thing, you ought to learn how to play it right.” And I started with the principal bassist in the symphony at the time in Cincinnati, when I was still in high school. And then I continued studying with the bow. That first teacher was Harold Roberts, who was the principal, and then I studied with Frank Proto in Cincinnati, who had just come from New York and joined the orchestra there. And then when I moved to Manhattan I studied with Orin O’Brien, who is a lady bassist in the philharmonic. So I continued to study through the years. And then my work with Gene Bertoncini, because he wanted to do a lot of things with the bow, kind of forced me into doing it in public, which was the kind of thing you had to practice at home, and I was afraid to play solos in particular, out. But working with him kind of encouraged me to do that. It made me work on it more.
